articles.title: A Spanish vineyard has gone more than 20 years without irrigation or pesticides; its cover-cropped topsoil now has over twice the organic matter of nearby tilled soil
articles.summary: Science News: For more than two decades, the soil between rows of grapevines in a Spanish vineyard has remained covered with spontaneous vegetation instead of being.
articles.body: For more than two decades, the soil between rows of grapevines in a Spanish vineyard has remained covered with spontaneous vegetation instead of being repeatedly tilled. The unusual approach was associated with a striking difference beneath the vines: soil managed with long-term vegetation cover contained more than twice as much organic matter in its top layer as nearby soil that was conventionally tilled. The finding offers a glimpse into how leaving the ground undisturbed and maintaining plant cover could help improve soil health in dry, water-limited vineyards. The findings come from a 2026 study published in Frontiers in Soil Science, which compared a rainfed vineyard in central Spain managed with spontaneous cover cropping for more than 20 years with an adjacent vineyard managed through conventional tillage. Researchers examined physical, chemical and biological characteristics of the soils, including organic matter, porosity, water retention, nutrients and microbial activity.Two different ways of managing soilThe study was conducted near Mota del Cuervo in Cuenca province, in central Spain. The region has a semi-arid Mediterranean climate, making water availability an important challenge for vineyards. According to the study, the farmer reported managing one of the vineyards for more than two decades without irrigation, pesticides or other external inputs. Instead of repeatedly removing vegetation between the grapevines, the farmer allowed spontaneous plants to grow and maintain ground cover. Vegetation was manually removed only immediately around individual vines.The neighbouring vineyard followed a much more conventional approach. Its soil was tilled regularly; researchers noted that vineyards in the region typically undergo several tillage operations each year to control weeds and maintain bare soil. This created a useful comparison because the two plots were adjacent and had comparable soil conditions. Rather than comparing vineyards from completely different environments, the researchers could examine how contrasting management practices were associated with differences in soil properties.Organic matter more than doubledThe clearest difference appeared in the amount of organic matter contained in the topsoil. Researchers found an average organic matter content of 1.74% in the topsoil under spontaneous cover cropping, compared with 0.83% in the conventionally tilled soil. That means the covered soil contained slightly more than twice the organic matter of the tilled comparison. Organic matter is an important component of healthy soil. It comes largely from decomposing plant and animal material and contributes to processes that influence soil structure, nutrient cycling and water behaviour.The researchers also found differences in soil structure. At depths of 10 to 30 centimetres, soil under long-term cover cropping had porosity of about 51.2%, compared with 44.0% under tillage. The cover-cropped soil also showed greater biological activity, with several enzyme activities elevated compared with the conventionally managed soil. The results suggest that keeping vegetation on the ground for long periods can gradually alter the soil environment. Plant roots continually add organic material, while fallen vegetation decomposes at the surface. At the same time, reduced soil disturbance may allow soil structure and biological communities to develop with less disruption.A possible lesson for dry vineyardsThe findings are particularly relevant because vineyards in Mediterranean regions often face a difficult combination of limited rainfall, soil degradation and the need to control vegetation around crops. Conventional tillage can keep vineyard rows visibly bare, but repeated disturbance can also break apart soil aggregates and accelerate organic matter loss. Cover crops offer an alternative by keeping living vegetation on the soil for at least part of the year and reducing the amount of bare ground exposed to wind and water erosion. Previous research has similarly linked ground cover with improvements in soil organic carbon, aggregate stability and infiltration.However, the study does not suggest that cover cropping is automatically suitable for every vineyard. Plants growing between vines can compete with grapevines for water, particularly in dry climates. Recent research in Mediterranean vineyards has found that cover crops can sometimes reduce vine growth under severe drought conditions. That makes the Spanish vineyard studied in Frontiers in Soil Science particularly interesting. It represents a long-running real-world example of how a farmer maintained spontaneous vegetation without irrigation or pesticides and allowed the soil to develop under relatively low disturbance for more than 20 years.Rather than treating every plant growing between the vines as a problem to be removed, the system allowed vegetation to become part of the vineyard's soil-management strategy. According to researchers, their findings support the idea that long-term spontaneous cover cropping can improve soil structure, organic matter and biological functioning in semi-arid vineyards. The results do not prove that the practice will eliminate the need for irrigation everywhere, but they show how maintaining living ground cover can potentially strengthen the soil's ability to function under challenging conditions. For vineyards facing increasing pressure from drought and soil degradation, the lesson is relatively simple: sometimes, healthier soil may begin with disturbing it less and allowing plants to remain.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Edwin Hubble: “Equipped with his five senses, man explores the universe around…”
articles.summary: Science News: One thing that characterises science in its early stages is the fact that it all starts with the desire to find out more about something that is yet u.
articles.body: One thing that characterises science in its early stages is the fact that it all starts with the desire to find out more about something that is yet unknown to people. As Edwin Hubble put it in one of his famous quotes, “Equipped with his five senses, man explores the universe around him and calls the adventure Science.” In this quote, the author shows how science should be viewed as something that goes far beyond mere numbers and equations. In other words, this is something that involves a continuous exploration of the world around us. Thus, we discover things and gradually learn through our observations and experiences.Edwin Hubble (1889-1953) was an American astronomer whose observations have changed the way humanity perceives the universe around it. His works have shown that there are many galaxies beyond our galaxy and that these galaxies move away from us.Quote of the day by Edwin Hubble“Equipped with his five senses, man explores the universe around him and calls the adventure Science”What does this quote mean?The quotation by Hubble implies that science is an approach which starts with observations. Human senses give us opportunities to see, listen, feel and experience the world, while scientific instruments help people go much further and observe things which are inaccessible through our senses. With telescopes we can observe distant galaxies, with microscopes we can observe structures which are invisible to naked eye and with scientific devices scientists can observe phenomena which cannot be perceived with human senses. And all this adventure starts with the observation of something and a question of why this phenomenon takes place.Curiosity is where scientific discovery beginsPrior to carrying out the experiment, there is usually a question. What makes stars glow? How do organisms evolve over generations? What happens in an atom? Is there anything beyond the universe which can be seen by a human being? These and many other questions were the basis for scientists who investigated the things which were unknown before. And Hubble’s explanation of science as an adventure shows this exploratory process of science very well. Sometimes unexpected discoveries are made.Our senses are only the beginningAlthough there are five basic senses, science has found incredible ways to enhance human senses. Radio telescopes can see things unseen by our eyes, gravitational wave detectors can see ripples in spacetime, and particle detectors can show the behavior of matter on microscopic scales. In this respect, scientific equipment has turned into an extension of human senses. This allows us to probe parts of the real world which would otherwise be inaccessible for our body.Hubble's own work changed our view of the universeHubble knew the power of scientific observation through his research as well. Through the study of galaxies far away from us, he showed that the universe is much greater than our galaxy. Furthermore, his observations provided additional proof that the universe is expanding. The small number of stars has been replaced by an unimaginably large space populated by innumerable galaxies. Improved observation methods changed our perception of where humanity is located within the universe.Every discovery reveals another mysteryWhat I find most interesting in science is that answering one question does not mark the end of the journey. Quite the opposite, it opens up a lot of new questions. The moment one learns the universe is expanding, there come many more questions about how that happened, how it developed and where will it all end? When one learns about cell activity, there come many more questions about consciousness and living organisms. When one learns about gravity, there come many more questions about its connection to quantum physics. The more people explore, the bigger becomes the field of the unknown.Science is a journey rather than a finished book“Adventure”, used by Hubble in his speech, means movement, unpredictability and discovery. Science is not much different. Scientists start from knowledge they already have, learn how to study the unknown and sometimes find out that their initial assumptions were wrong. Therefore, scientific knowledge is ever changing, based on the evidence found.Human curiosity can reach across unimaginable distancesThere is something extraordinary about the fact that humans can investigate objects billions of light-years away despite living on a small planet. Light travelling across the universe can be captured by instruments on Earth and transformed into information about stars, galaxies and cosmic events that happened long before human civilisation existed.That ability is perhaps exactly the kind of adventure Hubble had in mind. We do not have to physically travel somewhere to begin exploring it. Sometimes, observation itself is enough to take us there.Why this quote still matters todayHubble's words remain relevant because the fundamental impulse behind science has not changed. We continue to look, question, test and explore. The tools have become vastly more sophisticated, but the motivation remains deeply human, we want to understand what is around us. The enduring lesson behind his quote is that science is not simply about accumulating knowledge. It is the adventure of turning curiosity into discovery, and recognising that every new answer may reveal an even larger universe of questions waiting to be explored.

articles.title: In the 1930s, Texas built 3 bird-nesting islands from dredged mud; all vanished, but one rebuilt 4.5-acre island now hosts more than 2,500 nesting pairs
articles.summary: Science News: Dickinson Bay lost its charm over the decades. The small estuarine pocket on Galveston Bay's western shore once hosted thriving colonies of waterbirds.
articles.body: Dickinson Bay lost its charm over the decades. The small estuarine pocket on Galveston Bay's western shore once hosted thriving colonies of waterbirds on three dredged islands. But then the islands completely vanished. During the 1980s and 1990s, subsidence, erosion, and a string of tropical storms swept the islands beneath the water. And with them went crucial nesting grounds for terns, herons, pelicans, and gulls. But then people who cared about them brought them back.How Galveston Bay brought its birds backIn the 1930s, three islands were built in Dickinson Bay, using material dredged from the channel. But by the 1990s, all three islands had disappeared. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (Service) Coastal Program, which has long monitored the colonial waterbirds, saw a chance to restore the lost habitat. So, in the early 2000s, the Texas Coastal Program and the Galveston Bay restoration community started to look at ways to restore the islands of Dickinson Bay.In 2005 came the first glimmer of hope, when the Galveston Bay Foundation attempted to reconstruct the first of the three lost islands. Dickinson Bay Island I was created with approximately two acres of nesting space. Within weeks, birds arrived. Royal terns, sandwich terns, laughing gulls, and many other species that hadn’t been to the bay in years showed up. This arrival was proof enough that their restoration efforts were successful.In 2011, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Coastal Program contributed $50,000 to begin serious planning for a second, larger island. The funding was modest by restoration standards.What unfolded over the next ten years was phenomenal. The Galveston Bay Estuary Program joined. Restore America's Estuaries brought expertise. NOAA contributed planning support. Each organisation brought something different to the table. Think engineers, restoration ecologists, permitting specialists, and people who knew exactly how to navigate the bureaucracy of constructing on water.The real turning point came in 2017, when the Texas Trustee Implementation Group came in to fund the restoration, including final engineering and design and regulatory permitting. Construction began in late 2021 and was completed in May 2022. The result was breathtaking. A new 4.5-acre island, engineered to slope gradually into the water, was designed to accommodate species with different nesting needs and preferences. The efforts didn’t stop there. They also restored one acre of oyster reef and more than 2,000 trees and shrubs across the island. This acted as a protective structure and also provided habitat for oysters and fisheries that would benefit the local economies.The birds came backThe birds came before the official inaugural ceremony. They arrived early and caught even optimistic planners off guard. By spring 2025, the number of breeding pairs observed during this nesting season exceeded the Trustees' expectations. More than 2,500 pairs of waterbirds were estimated to be nesting on the island. Think of all kinds of waterbirds: great blue herons, little blue herons, snowy egrets, brown pelicans, roseate spoonbills, white ibises, cattle egrets, and tricoloured herons. So many visitors arrived, and the names look like a catalogue of Galveston Bay's biological wealth.The full investment topped $6 million. That's not an unusual number for coastal restoration at scale. The money didn’t go into a single contractor’s pocket either. It moved through supply chains, job sites, and specialised trades. Engineers designed. GIS specialists mapped. Survey crews measured. Heavy equipment operators moved earth. Tugboat crews towed barges. Fuel suppliers, concrete providers, marine construction specialists, you name it. The project not only saved the waterbirds but also became a source of temporary employment for thousands of people. In rural areas, seasonal work often leaves winter quiet, but this restoration project offered a genuine opportunity, which also helped the local economy.The restored island also provides scope for recreational fishing. That activity undoubtedly serves the economy. Think bait shops, fishing tackle retailers, boat maintenance, fuel suppliers, and the whole infrastructure that supports people spending a day on the water. With the assistance of the Service’s Economic Branch, the Coastal Program assessed its nearly $11.13 million in personnel and project expenditures for Fiscal Year 2025. What they found was striking. The Coastal Program expenditures supported 139 jobs and generated more than $30 million in economic output nationwide.The island is more than restored waterbird habitat. It is everything the locals can hope for. There are oyster reefs and fish habitat. It also provides recreational opportunities. It has also fed the locals with the jobs it created. Dickinson Bay Island II is the answer to everything that’s impossible. They built the islands even when nature wasn’t in their favour. By 2022, the birds had returned to the nests and have kept coming back ever since to their home.

articles.title: Musk vs. Altman: SpaceX stock in focus as OpenAI ends Cursor access to AI models
articles.summary: SpaceX stock is in focus on Monday after big news over the weekend concerning its AI coding tool Cursor and OpenAI.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock is in focus on Monday after big news over the weekend concerning its AI coding tool Cursor and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ).

OpenAI said late Friday evening that Cursor would no longer be allowed access to its AI models. SpaceX closed its acquisition of Cursor earlier this month in a $60 billion deal.

"We notified SpaceX that we intend to wind down our contract providing OpenAI models to Cursor, with a proposed shutoff date of November 12, 2026," OpenAI said . "We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts."

Despite the decision, SpaceX stock was higher in early trading.

OpenAI added more context to the complaints: "After Musk acquired Twitter, now part of SpaceX, the company broke⁠ the terms of our contract (alongside many others). Under oath earlier this year, Musk admitted that xAI, now also part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI's terms of service (terms which are similar to xAI's own)."

The Cursor move is the latest escalation in a war between Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Earlier this year, Musk sued OpenAI and Altman, claiming they betrayed the company's ​original nonprofit mission by creating a for-profit entity, among other things. A jury ruled against Musk, finding that he had filed ‌the ⁠case too late.

As for cutting off access to Cursor, Musk said he "couldn't care less."

This is a big issue for Cursor clients as they can no longer use OpenAI models, including its upcoming frontier model, Astra, for developer use. Michael Truell, Cursor's co-founder, said the two sides are speaking and looking to resolve the issue. Truell said 5% of Cursor traffic uses OpenAI models.

AI is a big part of SpaceX's future revenue growth, as the company projected in its IPO filing that it sees the AI opportunity worth potentially $26.5 trillion in the long term.

As for SpaceX's traditional rocket and launch business, it also suffered a small setback.

Over the weekend, NASA said it and SpaceX would be "adjusting the launch date" for NASA's upcoming Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station, which would carry four astronauts as part of the mission.

NASA and SpaceX said an "oxidizer leak" in the Dragon spacecraft's propulsion system was detected, and additional tests are needed to resolve the issue. The original launch target was Sept. 12. A new launch date has not been set.

Pras Subramanian is Lead Transportation Reporter for Yahoo Finance. You can follow him on X and on Instagram .

articles.title: Nobel Prize, Israel Prize laureate, Ada Yonath, dies aged 87
articles.summary: Professor Ada Yonath won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 and the Israel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. She was born in Jerusalem and worked at Weizmann Ins...
articles.body:
Professor Ada Yonath won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 and the Israel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. She was born in Jerusalem and worked at Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot.

Professor Ada Yonath, who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 and the Israel Prize in Chemistry in 2002, died on Monday at age 87.

Born in Jerusalem, Yonath worked at the Weizmann Institute of Science , Rehovot's Structural Biology and Chemistry Department, where she led the Ribosome Group, according to the institute's website.

A ribosome is a "tiny particle made up of RNA and proteins that specialize in protein synthesis and are found free or bound to the endoplasmic reticulum within cells," according to the Encyclopedia Britannica .

She was the daughter of Polish immigrants, whose father tried to earn a living by running a grocery store, despite having qualifications as a rabbi, according to a biography on the Nobel Prize website.

The Yonath family moved to Tel Aviv after her father passed away, and Ada studied chemistry at the bachelor's and master's levels at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem , graduating in 1962 and 1964, respectively. She later earned her PhD from the Weizmann Institute in 1968, researching X-ray crystallography.

She was elected a member of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 2000 and the US National Academy of Sciences in 2003, according to the Encyclopedia Britannica .

"An organism's vital functions are managed by large, complex protein molecules produced in cells' ribosomes. There, genetic information from messenger RNA is translated into chains of amino acids that then build proteins. In the 1970s, Ada Yonath began a project that culminated in 2000 in her successful mapping (together with other researchers) of the structure of ribosomes, which consist of hundreds of thousands of atoms, using x-ray crystallography. Among other applications, this has been important in the production of antibiotics," the Nobel Prize biography said, describing her work.

President Herzog eulogizes Israeli award-winning chemist

"I am deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Professor Ada Yonath, Nobel laureate in Chemistry, Wolf Prize laureate, Israel Prize laureate, and one of the leading researchers in the history of Israeli science," President Isaac Herzog said.

"Anyone who followed Professor Yonath's scientific journey knew that she was an international trailblazer, and a pioneer who proved that curiosity, dedication, and unwavering determination can push back the frontiers of human knowledge. Her groundbreaking discoveries changed the face of science and brought great honor to the State of Israel," he added.

"Professor Yonath lived out that very aspiration, serving as an inspiration to countless women and men alike. We will remember her for her modesty, the originality of her thinking, and as a role model and inspiration to generations of scientists in Israel and around the world. I send my deepest condolences to her family, her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science, her students, and the entire scientific community. May her memory be a blessing," he stated.

Weizmann Institute eulogizes Prof. Yonath

"Professor Yonath is an example and a role model for how scientific vision, courage in choosing a great scientific question, and dedication to a goal can lead to tremendous success and expand the boundaries of knowledge for the future of all humanity. May her memory be a blessing," the Weizmann Institute said in a statement.

"Ada was an exceptional scientist who never hesitated to choose a path that others considered impossible and to pursue it for decades with determination, curiosity and courage. Her breakthrough in the study of the ribosome transformed our understanding of one of life's most fundamental processes and opened up new possibilities for combating antibiotic resistance," Weizmann Institute President Prof. Alon Chen said.

"But Ada's legacy extends far beyond her scientific achievements. She showed generations of scientists what can be accomplished when one dares to ask big questions and persists in the search for answers. Ada was an Institute Professor – the highest title the Weizmann Institute bestows on a select group of outstanding scientists – and she continued to conduct research and publish papers, run an active laboratory and maintain scientific collaborations until the very last days of her life," Chen added.

articles.title: Meet Prakhar Purohit, the North Carolina student who found a way to make tiny batteries from dirty water
articles.summary: Science News: Prakhar Purohit, a student from North Carolina, has earned recognition for a science project with a unique yet simple-sounding idea of ‘making tiny ba.
articles.body: Prakhar Purohit, a student from North Carolina, has earned recognition for a science project with a unique yet simple-sounding idea of ‘making tiny batteries from dirty water.’ His project, titled ‘Tiny Batteries from Dirty Water,’ was selected as the 2026 North Carolina State Merit Winner in the 3M Young Scientist Challenge. The recognition places Purohit among students across the United States whose projects tackle different problems through science and technology. According to the Young Scientist Lab, the 2026 State Merit Winners have been announced as part of its annual challenge, which encourages students to work on real-world challenges that matter to them. Purohit’s project stands out because it connects two everyday concerns, dirty water and the need for small sources of electrical power, through a compact scientific idea. By exploring this unusual connection, the student shows how familiar environmental problems can inspire practical experiments with potential applications beyond the classroom.What did Prakhar Purohit createThe project is called ‘Tiny Batteries from Dirty Water.’ This title captures the central idea in just a few words. Rather than treating dirty water simply as something that needs to be cleaned or avoided, the project explores it as part of a battery-making concept. The Young Scientist Lab does not provide a detailed explanation of the design, materials or testing process. Still, the idea is notable for the way it appears to combine an environmental problem with a need for energy.Small batteries are useful in many areas of modern life, particularly where tiny devices need a source of power. Purohit’s project takes that familiar technology and looks at dirty water as the fuel. The Young Scientist Lab describes its Young Scientist Challenge as a programme designed to give students from different backgrounds a direct connection to innovation. It encourages them to tackle real-world challenges that are important to them through hands-on learning tools. Purohit’s project fits naturally into that broader goal. It attempts to look at a common environmental resource in a different way and ask whether something that is normally considered waste or a problem could also have a useful purpose. That kind of thinking is at the heart of student science projects. Instead of beginning with a ready-made answer, a young researcher can begin with a question that seems simple but opens the door to experimentation.How does dirty water become part of the ideaThe most important point is that Purohit’s project is specifically centred on dirty water. The project presents dirty water as something with potential value rather than simply as a contaminant. That is an interesting shift in perspective. A material that might normally be associated with pollution becomes the starting point for an investigation into energy. For a student project, the concept also shows how environmental questions can overlap with engineering. Water quality and energy are often discussed separately, but Purohit’s project brings the two subjects together under one idea. It asks whether dirty water can play a role in producing useful electrical power on a very small scale. That question is enough to make the project memorable. For Purohit, the 2026 State Merit Winner recognition marks an important achievement in his young scientific journey. For readers, the project offers a reminder that interesting scientific ideas do not always begin with complicated equipment or enormous labs. Sometimes, they begin with looking at an everyday problem differently.What does becoming a State Merit Winner meanPurohit was named the 2026 North Carolina State Merit Winner by the Young Scientist Lab. His project appears in the organisation’s official list alongside State Merit Winners from other states. The list includes projects covering a wide range of subjects. Other 2026 winners are working on ideas involving smoke detectors, traffic lights, lead detection, robotic therapy, plant communication and environmental technology. Purohit’s project therefore forms part of a much wider collection of student-led ideas. Each project approaches a problem from a different direction, but together they show the variety of questions young scientists are willing to explore.

articles.title: South Korea researchers turn 18,700 tons of kimchi radish waste into bioplastic
articles.summary: Each year, South Korea's kimchi industry uses roughly 145,000 tons of radish.
articles.body:
What if scientists figured out a way to transform food waste into a biodegradable plastic?

Researchers at the World Institute of Kimchi have done just that, developing a method for turning discarded radish by-products from kimchi production into bioplastic.

The breakthrough could potentially give a costly waste stream from one of South Korea's signature foods a far more useful second life.

The researchers detailed their findings in a study published in the journal Bioresource Technology .

According to Phys.org , the process of turning radish scraps into bioplastic involves using engineered E. coli bacteria to consume certain chemical components in the kimchi-processing leftovers, generating a biodegradable plastic that microorganisms can break down naturally.

If implemented at an industrial scale, the new method has the potential not only to provide a more environmentally friendly plastic alternative, but also to significantly reduce biowaste.

Each year, South Korea's kimchi industry uses roughly 145,000 tons of radish, leaving behind 18,700 tons of inedible residue. Over 90% of these leftovers end up in waste-treatment facilities, which is both costly for kimchi-makers and bad for the environment.

However, the new findings suggest that it might be possible to develop a circular economy that turns these agricultural by-products into a material with commercial value.

Biodegradable plastics could help reduce plastic pollution that lingers in landfills and the environment, while lowering waste-handling costs for manufacturers. If scaled, technology like this could support cleaner production systems and reduce the incentives to keep producing virgin fossil-fuel-based plastic.

The work also reflects a significant shift in science and manufacturing, with waste increasingly being treated as a resource rather than an expensive burden.

The research relied on advanced modeling to make low-waste manufacturing development more efficient. Using biological data alongside a genome-scale model, the team built an approach that could also be used to engineer microbes for other agricultural by-products beyond kimchi-radish waste.

Greater precision in microbe engineering could reduce development time and make sustainable materials more economically realistic. The more efficiently companies can convert leftovers into useful products, the easier it becomes to justify investments in cleaner manufacturing.

Consumers can also help create demand for alternatives to conventional plastic by choosing plastic-free options for everyday products .

articles.title: India's abandoned fishing village shows why more than just new homes are needed after natural disasters
articles.summary: In 2024, sudden climate hazards displaced about 8 million people in India and Bangladesh alone.
articles.body:
The deserted homes in a once-thriving Indian fishing village stand as a physical reminder of what happens when climate pressures push people inland, uprooting entire communities and disrupting traditional ways of life.

The former residents of Old Podampetta, situated along the country's east coast, have been driven out of their village by increasingly powerful cyclones and shoreline erosion. While many have attempted to build new lives elsewhere, research has found that successful relocation requires much more than just a new home.

According to The Conversation , studies of climate relocation in Bangladesh and India suggest that government programs implementing so-called "managed retreat" often fall short of providing the comprehensive support that effective relocation requires.

The findings are significant considering the massive number of people projected to be displaced due to the changing climate and rising sea levels.

In 2024, sudden climate hazards displaced about 8 million people in India and Bangladesh alone, the publication reported.

Of these millions of displaced evacuees, many do eventually return home. However, others cannot, often because erosion, flooding, and storm damage have left their communities too unsafe to rebuild.

The research indicated that to make permanent relocation a success, individuals must have the opportunity not only to have a new home, but also to recover lost livelihoods, relationships, and a sense of belonging. Without those things, even a move away from physical danger can leave families stuck dealing with other kinds of hardship, such as extreme poverty and a lack of access to necessary resources.

Because of this, managed-retreat policies that prioritize physical safety alone can ultimately end up worsening inequality rather than helping communities build a more secure future.

When approached correctly, relocation can improve life in important ways for some families.

For example, one interviewee living in Bangladesh's Khulna district described the relief of finally having a stable place to live.

"Earlier, we were living as tenants," the person explained, per The Conversation. "We lived in other people's houses. From time to time, we lived in different places. We did not have a settlement in one place. We did not have a fixed house."

Having a formal, permanent address can make it easier to access government benefits, obtain legal recognition, apply for loans, and participate in skills training.

For many transplants, however, escaping climate danger can bring a different set of problems, including isolation, poor infrastructure, and fewer ways to make a living.

Some households that had previously been able to rely on growing their own vegetables and fishing in nearby waters have found themselves forced to pay for food.

"We have to buy everything here," one displaced individual told researchers, per The Conversation. "We never had to buy rice, vegetables, or fish [in the place where we lived before]."

By conducting fieldwork among relocated communities in Bangladesh and India, researchers have begun to better understand the factors that lead to successful climate retreat. Throughout the two countries, they found uneven outcomes: Some relocated households gained better housing or market access, while others lost farmland, forests, fishing grounds, or informal work.

The findings led the researchers to conclude that successful relocation programs require meaningful community input, fair compensation, usable roads, and a plan for earning an income after the move.

Additionally, the researchers concluded that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to climate relocation. The outcome depends on specific details like where people move, what work they can find there, and whether essential services are accessible.

The image of Old Podampetta, the abandoned fishing village, serves as a symbol of the challenges facing relocated communities, as well as a reminder that some of what they have lost can never be regained.

As one study participant told the researchers, "Is there a greater sadness than having to leave the place of your birth?"

articles.title: Nasa scientists grew corn seeds in space and found that microgravity changed how the seedlings’ roots and shoots grew
articles.summary: Science News: Long before astronauts ever plant a seed on the Moon or Mars, Nasa has been testing a much simpler question here on Earth's doorstep: what happens whe.
articles.body: Long before astronauts ever plant a seed on the Moon or Mars, Nasa has been testing a much simpler question here on Earth's doorstep: what happens when a corn seed germinates with no gravity to tell it which way to grow? Back in the early 1990s, researchers flew dry corn kernels aboard the space shuttle, let them sprout in orbit, and compared them against identical seedlings grown under normal gravity on the ground. The plants survived. Their tissue looked healthy. But something was clearly missing. Without gravity acting as a compass, the roots and shoots lost their sense of direction entirely, growing in tangled, unpredictable patterns instead of the neat, downward and upward paths seen on Earth. It is a small but telling result, and one that Nasa has kept building on ever since, through experiments on corn and a range of other plants aboard the International Space Station.What happened to corn seeds in space without gravityOne of the clearest examples comes from a Nasa-funded shuttle experiment described in a 1992 paper archived on the agency's Technical Reports Server, hosted by Nasa's Kennedy Space Centre. Researchers imbibed dry corn kernels, launched them into orbit, and allowed them to germinate and grow for five days in darkness, comparing the seedlings against identical batches grown under normal gravity on Earth.According to Nasa, the shuttle-grown seedlings developed largely as expected in terms of weight, hormone levels, and tissue structure, but with one striking exception. As per the researchers, the tissues of the shuttle-grown plants appeared normal, and the seedlings differed only in the lack of orientation of roots and shoots. In other words, the plants grew perfectly healthy tissue; they simply could not tell which way to point it.How does gravity guide plant growthOn Earth, gravity gives a germinating seed an unambiguous cue: roots grow down, shoots grow up. Remove that cue, and a seedling has to rely on other signals, such as light, moisture gradients, or its own internal mechanical sensing, to decide which direction to grow. The corn experiment showed that when gravity disappears, roots and shoots stop following a single consistent path and instead grow in a jumble of directions, an effect popularly described as roots and shoots losing their orientation, or growing in twisted, disorganised patterns rather than the straight lines seen on Earth.Crucially, the Nasa researchers were cautious about over-interpreting a five-day snapshot. As per the paper, the findings could not be extrapolated to growth in microgravity for weeks, months, and years, of the kind that might be needed aboard a future space station or transit vehicle to Mars. The seedlings looked healthy over five days; nobody yet knew what would happen over five months.Do other plants also lose direction in spaceCorn is far from the only species to show this kind of directional confusion in orbit. Nasa-funded experiments using Arabidopsis thaliana, a small mustard-family plant that is the workhorse of plant spaceflight biology, have repeatedly documented roots that "skew" or curve away from a straight growth path once gravity is removed. According to a 2020 study published in Frontiers, titled ‘Root Skewing-Associated Genes Impact the Spaceflight Response of Arabidopsis thaliana’, in Plant Science and conducted aboard the International Space Station, this skewing behaviour was long assumed to require gravity as a reference point, and the observation that it persists in orbit overturned that assumption.A separate Nasa-supported ISS experiment, known as CARA, reached a similar conclusion from a different angle: gene activity rather than visible shape. As per the 2024 paper published in Nature, titled ‘Light has a principal role in the Arabidopsis transcriptomic response to the spaceflight environment’, plant tissue grown on the space station showed distinctive patterns of gene switching depending on whether it was exposed to light or kept in darkness, reflecting a complex, tissue-specific effort by the plant to reorganise its own growth machinery in the absence of gravity. Taken together with the corn results, the pattern across species is consistent: plants do not fail in microgravity, but they do lose their built-in compass.How is Nasa preparing to grow food in spaceThe agency has built an entire open-access infrastructure specifically to capture and share findings like these. The Open Science Data Repository serves as a one-stop location for a variety of the agency's space biological data, consolidating decades of plant, animal, and human spaceflight research from Nasa's Ames Life Sciences Data Archive and GeneLab databases into a single searchable system.That matters because Nasa's plans for long-duration missions, including eventual crewed trips to Mars, assume astronauts will be able to grow at least part of their own food along the way. Understanding exactly how and why plants lose their sense of direction in microgravity, while still growing healthy tissue as the corn experiment showed, is a necessary step towards designing growth systems, lighting cues, or even genetic tweaks that can compensate for the missing gravity signal before crews ever depend on space-grown crops for survival.

articles.title: Scientists discover how snails turn mucus into five different materials using calcium, collagen VI and changing protein levels
articles.summary: Science News: Snails may move slowly, but the mucus they produce is far more sophisticated than it looks. It has been revealed how grove snails can fine-tune this s.
articles.body: Snails may move slowly, but the mucus they produce is far more sophisticated than it looks. It has been revealed how grove snails can fine-tune this sticky substance for different purposes. Researchers identified five distinct mucus-based materials, each with its own mechanical properties and function. One helps the snails move smoothly by reducing friction, while another allows them to attach firmly to surfaces. Two others serve as defensive materials, helping the animals respond to threats. The fifth forms a mineral-rich layer that seals the shell during dormancy. A new research article published in Science titled ‘Calcium tunes snail mucus–based materials to multiple functions’ found that calcium plays an important role in creating these differences, working alongside structural proteins to alter the behaviour of the mucus. By adjusting the composition of a shared set of ingredients, the snails can produce materials that lubricate, stick, protect or harden.How can one snail produce five types of mucusResearchers studied grove snails, Cepaea nemoralis, and identified five forms of mucus, each serving a different purpose. The first is a lubricant released beneath the foot, helping the snail move across surfaces with less friction. The second forms an adhesive film that allows the animal to attach itself firmly to surfaces. When threatened, the snail produces two types of defensive mucus: a thick yellow secretion and a bubbly foam. The fifth material, known as the epiphragm, forms a protective seal over the shell opening during dormancy. Despite their different functions and physical properties, all five materials are made from broadly similar ingredients, including water, glycoproteins and complex carbohydrates. Collagen VI was identified as an important structural protein. Researchers found that differences in protein and calcium levels help the snail transform this common chemical toolkit into materials with distinct properties and functions.Why is calcium so important to the snail’s mucusThe study found that calcium plays a central role in determining how snail mucus behaves. Researchers detected different concentrations of the mineral across the five mucus types and found calcium carbonate stored inside the glands that produce the secretions. In wet mucus, amorphous calcium carbonate can release calcium ions that interact with proteins in the mucus network. These interactions can alter the material’s response to mechanical stress. The epiphragm contains the highest calcium concentration at about 420 milligrams per gram, nearly 17 times higher than that of the lubricant. Researchers also found evidence that calcium carbonate can transform into calcite, helping strengthen the mineralised barrier and providing the dormant snail with additional protection.How do protein levels change the behaviour of snail slimeProtein concentration also helps determine how the snail’s mucus behaves. The lubricant contained only about 0.3% protein, while the yellow defensive mucus had roughly 4%. This difference affects how the materials respond to mechanical stress. The way mucus is physically organised also changes its final properties. The yellow defensive secretion forms a fibrous material, while collagen gathers around the bubbles in the defensive foam. The snail produces this foam by pushing air through its breathing opening. These findings suggest that the animal does more than release the same mucus for different purposes. It appears to regulate both the chemical composition and physical organisation of its secretions. By making these adjustments, the snail can turn similar basic ingredients into materials that lubricate, adhere, stretch or provide protection when needed.What scientists learned about the versatility of snail mucusThe findings could help scientists understand how nature creates materials with different properties from a relatively simple set of ingredients. The snail’s ability to alter its mucus from a slippery lubricant to a stronger material could offer ideas for developing new adhesives, protective coatings and materials for wound repair. By changing protein levels, calcium chemistry and the way the mucus is physically organised, the snail can produce substances suited to lubrication, adhesion, and mineral protection.

articles.title: Meet Aman Sanger, the 25-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneur whose AI startup Cursor is being acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX for $60 billion: From coding at 14 and MIT to a potential $2.7 billion fortune
articles.summary: A few years ago, Aman Sanger was a young MIT student working on ideas around artificial intelligence. Today, the 25-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneu.
articles.body: A few years ago, Aman Sanger was a young MIT student working on ideas around artificial intelligence. Today, the 25-year-old Indian-origin entrepreneur finds himself at the centre of one of the biggest AI deals of the year- after Elon Musk’s SpaceX agreed to acquire Anysphere, the company behind AI coding platform Cursor, in a deal valuing it at $60 billion.The deal has turned Sanger and his three co-founders into some of the youngest billionaires in the technology world. But the story of Cursor did not begin with a giant valuation or a Musk acquisition. It began with four young engineers trying to figure out what AI could do inside a programmer’s everyday workflow.Who is Aman Sanger?Sanger is one of the four co-founders of Anysphere, the company behind Cursor. He studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he met co-founders Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif and Arvid Lunnemark.According to an Outlook Business report, Sanger comes from a family with Indian roots. His father, Arvind Sanger, is an IIT Bombay alumnus who went on to work in the hedge-fund industry, while his mother, Shilpa Sanger, is an orthodontist and entrepreneur.Before building Anysphere, Sanger had already spent time at Bridgewater Associates and Google and had also worked on his own AI consulting venture. He now serves as Anysphere’s chief operating officer (COO).From an MIT idea to CursorAnysphere was founded in 2022 by Sanger, Asif, Truell and Lunnemark. Their initial experiments were not necessarily focused on building the coding assistant that Cursor would eventually become.The founders explored AI applications in areas including computer-aided design before turning their attention towards software development. Their central idea was relatively simple: instead of making programmers switch between their code editor and a separate AI chatbot, why not put AI directly into the coding environment? That idea became Cursor.Unlike conventional coding assistants that mainly suggest snippets of code, Cursor is designed to work with larger portions of a developer’s codebase. It can help generate and modify code, identify bugs and undertake complex programming tasks based on natural-language instructions.This also helped fuel the rise of what is popularly known as “vibe coding”- a style of software development in which people describe what they want in ordinary language and let AI handle much of the coding work.Why did SpaceX want Cursor?SpaceX had already begun working with Cursor before the acquisition. In April 2026, the two companies announced a broader collaboration, with SpaceX securing the option to either acquire Cursor for $60 billion or pay $10 billion for a partnership if the acquisition did not go ahead. SpaceX ultimately chose the acquisition route.The transaction will make Anysphere a wholly owned subsidiary of SpaceX, with Cursor shareholders receiving SpaceX Class A stock based on the $60-billion implied equity value, according to the US Securities and Exchange Commission filing cited by Outlook Business.The reason is also tied to Musk’s larger ambitions in artificial intelligence. SpaceX and Cursor had been working on a new AI model, which was expected to be used across Cursor as well as Grok, the AI chatbot developed by Musk’s xAI. In effect, the deal gives Musk’s AI ecosystem a ready-made product used by software developers, along with the young team that built it.How much is Aman Sanger worth after the deal?The $60-billion valuation has dramatically changed the financial fortunes of Cursor’s founders. According to Forbes, Sanger, Sualeh Asif, Michael Truell and Arvid Lunnemark each held roughly a 4.5% stake in Anysphere. Estimates put the value of each founder’s stake at around $2.7 billion following the acquisition. The deal has also benefited major investors in Anysphere, including Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital.The company’s rapid rise is particularly striking. Anysphere raised $2.3 billion in its previous major funding round, reaching a valuation of about $29.3 billion. Its business continued to expand rapidly as demand for AI-powered coding tools surged.From young founder to Musk’s AI ecosystemFor Sanger, the SpaceX deal marks a remarkable turn in a journey that began with an idea shared among four young MIT engineers.Cursor had grown into a tool used by tens of thousands of teams, including engineering organisations at companies such as Nvidia, Adobe, Uber, Shopify and PayPal, according to Outlook Business. The company also said its platform was being used across 64% of Fortune 500 companies.What makes the story stand out is the speed of that transformation. Anysphere was only founded in 2022. Within four years, its product had become valuable enough for SpaceX to put $60 billion behind it.For Sanger, the deal is therefore more than a lucrative exit. It is the latest chapter in a much larger shift in software development- one where the programmer increasingly tells the machine what to build, while AI handles more of the work required to make it happen. And now, that technology sits inside Elon Musk’s rapidly expanding AI ambitions.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Scientists tested spiders as living DNA traps; their stomach contents can reveal which insects and other animals are living around them
articles.summary: Science News: A study published in ‘Experimental and Applied Entomology’ has explored how spiders could tell what animals are living around them by examining traces.
articles.body: A study published in ‘Experimental and Applied Entomology’ has explored how spiders could tell what animals are living around them by examining traces of prey DNA left inside their bodies. The research tested how ‘reliable prey DNA’ could be found in wolf spiders after feeding and how long that genetic evidence remained detectable. The experiments showed that DNA from some prey could still be detected several days after a meal, although the chances fell as digestion progressed. The findings suggest that spiders could become useful biological samplers for studying food webs and the small creatures living in an area. At the same time, the research shows why timing and laboratory methods matter when scientists use a spider’s stomach contents as a window into their surroundings and nearby ecosystems too.Scientists can now identify a spider’s prey by analysing DNA from its bodySpiders are predators, so every meal can leave behind a small genetic record of what they have eaten. Instead of trying to observe every tiny insect in a habitat, scientists can examine the DNA remaining in a spider after it has consumed prey. The idea is particularly useful because spiders do not leave behind neat, recognisable pieces of food. As the study explains, spiders digest their prey externally and consume it in liquid form, which makes traditional analysis of what they have eaten difficult. DNA-based methods provide another way to identify those meals. The research by Jeffery Marker and colleagues at Karlstad University focused on wolf spiders belonging to the family Lycosidae. These spiders are generalist predators, meaning they can feed on a variety of prey. That makes them potentially useful for studying relationships between predators and the wider animal community.How the scientists prepared spiders before testing for DNAThe scientists wanted to answer a fairly practical question of ‘how long does prey DNA remain detectable inside a spider.’ To find out, they collected Pardosa spiders from forested areas in southern Sweden. The spiders were kept individually in lab containers and were given controlled meals. Three types of prey were used which included the fruit fly ‘Drosophila hydei,’ the cricket ‘Gryllus bimaculatus’ and the springtail ‘Coecobrya tenebricosa.’ Before feeding, the spiders were starved for at least 8 days, with the average starvation period being about 17 days. After the spiders had eaten, researchers examined different groups at intervals ranging from immediately after feeding to eight days later. In total, 203 spiders were included in the final analysis. This gave the researchers a controlled way to watch the genetic evidence of a meal gradually disappear.Method used by scientists to find the prey DNAThe team used a technique called ‘DNA metabarcoding.’ Put simply, it allows researchers to look for short pieces of genetic material and use them to work out which species they came from. The researchers tested two combinations of laboratory primers, which act like molecular starting points for copying a particular section of DNA. Both were designed to target a part of the ‘mitochondrial COI gene,’ a commonly used genetic region for identifying animals. One combination performed better than the other. The researchers therefore used the more successful pair for their DNA metabarcoding work. The difference mattered because prey DNA becomes increasingly broken down as digestion continues. A method that can detect shorter pieces of DNA can therefore be especially useful when the genetic material has already begun to degrade.How long could the spiders reveal what they had eatenThe results showed that time was the most important factor affecting whether prey DNA could still be detected. Using the more successful primer combination, Drosophila DNA could be detected for up to 120 hours, or five days, after feeding. Gryllus DNA could be detected for up to 96 hours, or four days. However, the likelihood of finding the DNA decreased as more time passed after the meal. The researchers calculated DNA detection half-lives of about 41.6 hours for Drosophila and 15.2 hours for Gryllus. In other words, the genetic evidence did not simply disappear at once. Instead, the likelihood of detecting it gradually declined. The third prey, Coecobrya, produced much weaker results. Its DNA was detected in fewer than 9% of the spiders, meaning there was not enough consistent evidence to calculate a reliable detection half-life.Mapping the animals in the spider’s ecosystemThe research does not show that spiders can immediately be used as complete surveys of every animal in an ecosystem. Instead, the study demonstrates that prey DNA can survive inside wolf spiders long enough to be detected using molecular techniques. That creates an opportunity for scientists to use predators as indirect sources of information about prey communities. A spider collected from a particular environment may carry genetic evidence of recent meals. By examining that evidence, researchers could potentially learn more about predator-prey relationships without having to find and identify every small animal directly. However, the study also highlights an important limitation. A negative DNA result does not necessarily mean that a particular prey species was absent. The genetic evidence may simply have degraded beyond detection, or the chosen laboratory method may not have worked equally well for that prey.Importance of timing of a spider’s mealThe study makes clear that a spider's stomach is not a permanent record. It is more like a short-lived biological diary. The longer the time between feeding and collection, the greater the chance that the prey's DNA will become difficult to detect. The choice of laboratory primers also matters. The researchers argue that future studies should take factors such as previous gut contents, starvation periods and possible differences in metabolism into account. The work by Marker and colleagues ultimately shows why a spider can be more than just a predator in an ecosystem study. Its latest meal can carry a small genetic record of the life around it. With careful sampling and the right DNA methods, those tiny traces could give scientists another way to understand the hidden communities of insects and other animals that are otherwise difficult to observe.

articles.title: Once hunted to near extinction, Brazil’s humpback whales make a stunning comeback, population surges from just 2,000 to nearly 35,000 in two decades
articles.summary: Science News: Humpback whales are returning in large numbers to Brazil’s coast after being pushed close to extinction by commercial whaling. Their population in the.
articles.body: Humpback whales are returning in large numbers to Brazil’s coast after being pushed close to extinction by commercial whaling. Their population in the South Atlantic has risen from about 2,000 to around 35,000 in roughly 40 years, bringing the species close to its population levels before large-scale whaling.According to Science X, the recovery is now clearly visible along Brazil’s coast, including around Rio de Janeiro’s Guanabara Bay where thousands of humpback whales pass through Brazilian waters every year during their migration. Their return has also increased interest in whale-watching trips.The warm waters off Brazil are an important breeding ground for Southern Atlantic humpbacks. Between June and November, the whales travel about 4,000 kilometres from feeding grounds in the Southern Ocean to breeding and calving areas off northeastern Brazil. Many gather around the Abrolhos Bank, a coral reef region along the coasts of Bahia and Espirito Santo.Not long ago, humpback whales were rarely seen in Brazilian waters. According to Enrico Marcovaldi, co-founder of the Humpback Whale Project and founder of the Humpback Whale Institute, four decades ago, people did not even know there were whales in Brazil.“The first time he saw one, he mistook it for a rock. They were legends. We had never seen one,” Marcovaldi said, as quoted by AFP.Whaling ban helped A major reason for the recovery was the reduction and eventual end of commercial whaling. In 1982, the International Whaling Commission decided that commercial whaling should be paused for all whale species and populations from the 1985/1986 season onwards. Brazil then banned commercial whaling by law in 1987.Brazil also protected the Abrolhos breeding grounds. These measures gave humpback whales greater protection during an important part of their life cycle. The species was removed from Brazil’s list of threatened species in 2014, and its population has continued to grow.Louise Raulais, who runs the Rio Ocean Club with her partner Theo Andrade, said their company began offering sailboat trips this year for groups of five to 10 people to watch humpback whales.A biologist travels on every trip and explains the whales and the ocean to visitors. Raulais said the experience can encourage people to care more about marine life.“These animals are so iconic and charismatic that they have the power to transform people, to change the way they see the world,” she said.Tracking whales through skin, photographsThe growing whale population is giving researchers more opportunities to study the animals. They travel to areas such as the Abrolhos archipelago to record the whales, study their behaviour and health, and understand their movements.Biologist Fabio Fontes collects skin and blubber samples from whales using an arrow. He follows groups of male humpbacks competing to mate with a female and takes samples from individual animals.These samples can help establish family relationships between whales. Such information is useful because humpback whales are among the mammals known for travelling very long distances.Researchers previously found that a humpback born in the Abrolhos area was related to another whale seen near South Georgia, about 4,000 kilometres to the south. The discovery helped understand the migration route of these animals.Adult humpback whales can grow up to 16 metres long and weigh as much as six elephants. They feed on krill and small fish during the warmer months and move to tropical waters to breed during winter.Researchers also identify individual whales by studying the markings on their tails. The black-and-white pattern on each whale's tail is unique, much like a fingerprint.Earlier, comparing photographs to identify whales required researchers to spend hours looking through images. Now, an artificial intelligence platform called Happy Whale can make the comparison within seconds.The platform has already identified 8,300 Brazilian humpback whales. It also helped researchers identify a whale in Brazil that had previously been spotted more than 15,000 kilometres away off Australia's east coast. The finding was reported in research published in May.“We are seeing that populations in the Southern Hemisphere are much more interconnected than we imagined,” said Milton Marcondes, research coordinator at the Humpback Whale Institute.The return of the whales does not mean the species is free from danger. Researchers say humpback whales still face threats from maritime traffic and fishing nets. Warming seas linked to climate change are another concern because changes in ocean conditions can affect the krill on which the whales depend.

articles.title: A man bought 51,000 acres of degraded land in Florida; decades later, it became the largest private restoration project east of the Mississippi
articles.summary: Science News: He is 85, known as the father of sociobiology, has been at Harvard for 60 years, and has won a hundred scientific awards, including two Pulitzer Prize.
articles.body: He is 85, known as the father of sociobiology, has been at Harvard for 60 years, and has won a hundred scientific awards, including two Pulitzer Prizes. Yet what E.O. Wilson, an evolutionary biologist, is focused on is a new conservation approach, a new ecological Grail which is a quest to refute conservation sceptics who think there isn't enough left of the natural world to be worth saving, according to a report by Smithsonian Magazine.Through the 544 million years or so, since hard-shelled animals first appeared, there has been a gradual increase in the number of plants and animals on the planet, despite five mass extinction events. While the high point of biodiversity most likely coincided with the moment modern humans left Africa and spread across the globe, over the years, species faltered and vanished. It was slow at first, but now, the event is taking place at an acceleration where Wilson predicts the oncoming of a "biological holocaust," a sixth mass extinction event, caused by humans. According to him, the only way humans could prevent a mass extinction crisis would be to set aside half the planet as permanently protected for the ten million other species.While one would believe this to be a fantastical dream inspired by a dreamer, a forest being created by M.C. Davis, a multimillionaire, is already on the pathway. Davis's idea has been to revive the 'Piney Woods', the signature ecosystem of the American Southeast. The longleaf pine forest once covered 90 million acres, or about 60 per cent of the land, in a virtually continuous 1,200-mile stretch across nine states from Virginia to East Texas.That forest has been reduced by 97% and there are about three million acres of it left. The coral reefs have been destroyed by about 10-20% and the Amazon rainforest has been damaged by more than 20%. The longleaf pine forest’s “Big Cut,” as it’s still known, began after the Civil War and left behind what commentators referred to as “a sea of stumps.” Much of the land has since been reforested, but de-longleafed, and is now planted with row after row of faster-growing pines raised for pulpwood.Davis, who is a commodities trader in timber and oil and gas rights, and grew up about 65 miles west of his forest, has spent the past decade spending half a million dollars annually planting longleaf pine trees and another half million on other parts of a longleaf forest.His awakening for the cause came from a 'Black Bear Seminar' that he walked in on while being stuck in traffic. “There was an old drunk, and a politician who’d thought there’d be a crowd, and a couple of Canadians looking for day-old doughnuts and coffee—and, up on the stage, two women talking about saving black bears. They were riveting. The next day I gave those ladies enough money to keep going for another two years, which I think scared them, it was so out of the blue. Then I asked them for a 100-book environmental reading list for me, for my education. I spent a year reading Thoreau, John Muir, and Ed Wilson. Then I started buying up land to see what I could do,” he told the outlet.Saving the forests and the dwellersIf one was going to save Florida black bears, it was clear from the start, they’d have to save longleaf forests, their preferred habitat. An adult male black bear roams across perhaps a hundred square miles of land. North Florida already had some good-sized clusters of publicly owned longleaf—national forests, state forests, wildlife management areas and, in the western Panhandle, Eglin Air Force Base, a huge facility that back before World War II had itself been a national forest. The problem was that 70 miles separated the first two protected longleaf forests—and it was another 95 miles to the third.As he dug deeper, Davis realised that the coastal Southeast is a “hyper­diverse” biological hotspot with up to 60 different species in a single square yard. Davis planned to buy up and re-longleaf the “in-between” open space east of Eglin and west of a protected river corridor. He had his sights on a series of abandoned peanut farms and unproductive pulpwood forests with low asking prices.He bought 51,000 acres of degraded farms and forests, that barely included 1,500 acres of longleaf pines in scattered patches. He named the area Nokuse Plantation, pronounced 'No-GO-see' and meaning 'bear' in the language of the Muskogee people who once lived there. Nokuse is the biggest private preserve and the biggest restoration project east of the Mississippi.To honour Wilson, whom Davis credits as the inspiration for his effort, he built a $12 million E.O. Wilson Biophilia Center at one edge of Nokuse, where thousands of fourth through seventh graders from six counties get free classes that let them hold real baby gopher tortoises and clamber and pose for pictures on a giant ant sculpture.At Nokuse, Davis and his crew of workers have thinned 22,000 acres of pulpwood pines and planted eight million longleaf seedlings. He’s brought flames back to the woods after a half-century absence, setting carefully controlled fires on about 10,000 acres every year. Bears have reintroduced themselves in the area, ambling in from Eglin Air Force Base nearby. Davis is planning to bring back red-cockaded woodpeckers and bison.So far, Nokuse's proudest achievement has been the recruitment of the foot-long gopher tortoise. Nokuse Plantation director Matt Aresco, a biologist with a PhD in turtle studies, has retrieved 3,500 otherwise doomed gopher tortoises from all over Florida. These “ecosystem engineers,” as one conservation biologist calls them, have the kind of transforming influence on their surroundings that beaver families do.As of now, Nokuse still looks scruffy. “I tell people we’re in Year 13 of a 300-year program. I could easily make 1,000 acres look beautiful, but the extinction clock’s ticking, so I decided to take on the bigger challenge,” said Davis.
